\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for solver-backed formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
This gap is especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback, driving rapid prove-rate gains but providing no signal on structural quality.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and transfer poorly to arbitrary solver-backed settings; while LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}, RL training produces qualitatively different failures because the optimizer actively reshapes the output distribution toward degenerate attractors.
What is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in solver-backed formal outputs.

We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs to test whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary (Figure~\ref{fig:sta-overview}).
The fraction of necessary components yields the \emph{Irreducible Solver Rate} (ISR), where $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicates full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate: structural quality degrades by $99.5\%$ over 1000 steps while prove rate rises from $32\%$ to $96\%$ (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
An SFT baseline on identical data largely avoids hacking, consistent with hacking being associated with RL optimization rather than data exposure, though the large prove-rate gap prevents definitive causal attribution (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
The mechanism is structural: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive high ISR by construction, creating an attractor that eventually captures all seeds under extended training.
The effect transfers to Prolog with complete collapse through three distinct mechanisms (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

We present an empirical case study of Goodhart collapse in solver-backed RL, using FOLIO with Qwen3 (4B/1.7B) across six reward conditions, ten seeds (5+5 matched design), two logic types, and up to 1000 training steps. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{ISR as a structural diagnostic} for GRPO reward hacking that reveals a collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
  \item \textbf{Empirical characterization of Goodhart dynamics} under LOO-based rewards, including seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying patterns, and a taxonomy of eight automatically detected hacking modes plus one identified by manual audit (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}--\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
  \item \textbf{Cross-logic and cross-scale evidence} that Goodhart vulnerability transfers in principle across logic types and model scales, though coverage remains preliminary (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}--\ref{sec:crossscale}).
\end{enumerate}
These are cautionary results from a single model family and dataset: snapshot evaluation of structural rewards can overestimate their benefit; only trajectory analysis reveals the transient nature of apparent improvement.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Task and GRPO Training}
\label{sec:task}

Given premises $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ and conclusion $C$, the task is to produce a formal program $x=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$ verified by an external solver $S\in\{\text{Prover9}$~\citep{mccune-prover9}$, \text{SWI-Prolog}$~\citep{wielemaker2012swi}$\}$ .
We train with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}4$), where each rollout receives binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}(x) = \mathbf{1}[S(x){=}\textit{proved}]$.
This optimizes prove rate but provides no signal about \emph{structural quality}: a formalization embedding the conclusion among its premises receives the same reward as a faithful derivation.
All experiments draw from FOLIO~\citep{folio}; the held-out evaluation file retains a legacy \texttt{proofwriter\_fol\_*.jsonl} filename (from ProofWriter~\citep{proofwriter}) but contains only FOLIO-derived examples.

\subsection{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{sec:sta}

STA tests whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary for proof success .
Given a proved $x$ with $n$ components, STA constructs $n$ ablated variants $x\setminus\{c_i\}$ and re-runs the solver (Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta}).
A component is \emph{necessary} if its removal causes proof failure.
What constitutes a component depends on the logic: premises and conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent) in FOL, clauses or ground facts in Prolog.
For example, given premise $\forall x(R(x){\to}P(x))$ and conclusion $\forall x(P(x){\to}Q(x))$, the decomposition yields components $\{$premise, $\forall x$, $P(x)$, $Q(x)\}$ with $n{=}4$.
LOO ablation itself is standard in mutation testing and sensitivity analysis~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Proved formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE $\text{ISR}(x) \in [0, 1]$
\STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ to $n$}
    \IF{$S(x \setminus \{c_i\}) = \textit{failed}$}
        \STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets \textit{necessary} + 1$
    \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $\textit{necessary} \,/\, n$
\end{algorithmic}
\smallskip
{\footnotesize For FOL, components include both premises and conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent); each sub-expression is ablated by removing it from the solver input and testing whether the proof still succeeds.}
\end{algorithm}

ISR is the fraction of necessary components:
\begin{equation}
  \text{ISR}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\bigl[S(x\setminus\{c_i\})=\textit{failed}\bigr]
  \label{eq:isr}
\end{equation}
ISR is defined only for proved formalizations: ISR${=}1$ means every component is necessary; ISR${=}0$ means complete redundancy.
ISR is a component-necessity diagnostic, not a reasoning-quality metric; it measures whether each piece is needed for the proof, not whether the proof faithfully represents the original problem.
We report \emph{proved-only} ISR (denoted ISR$^*$) throughout to avoid conflating structural quality with prove rate.

ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a formalization can achieve $\text{ISR}{=}1$ while remaining semantically unrelated to the NL input.
ISR is sensitive to component count $n$: fewer components mechanically inflate ISR because each is more likely to be individually necessary.
This confound is central to ISR's Goodhart vulnerability (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): TS tautologies (single premise $=$ conclusion) achieve $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction; premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the apparent ISR advantage ($1.06\times$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
ISR functions as a diagnostic but fails as a training signal because optimization exploits the metric's structural bias rather than improving reasoning quality.

Shapley values~\citep{shapley-1953} account for interaction effects but cost $O(2^n)$; we chose LOO because it directly answers ``is this component necessary?'' at $O(n)$ cost.
A cheaper $O(1)$ binary variant produces near-zero ISR ($\text{ISR}^*{=}0.007$), confirming that per-clause LOO is necessary for ISR to carry a structural signal (Appendix~\ref{app:o1-ablation}).

\subsection{Reward Conditions and Hacking Modes}
\label{sec:rewards}
\label{sec:taxonomy-method}

We study six primary conditions.
The exec-only baseline uses binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}$ alone.
ISR reward augments execution with a structural bonus, $r = r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1{+}\beta\,\text{ISR})$, at primary doses $\beta\in\{0.1,0.3\}$ and supplementary points $\beta\in\{0.05,0.2\}$; matched random controls replace ISR with uniform noise ($r = r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1{+}\beta u)$, $u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$) to isolate ISR-specific signal from generic reward-variance effects.
An SFT baseline trained with negative log-likelihood on gold formalizations tests whether structural degeneration arises from RL optimization or data exposure.
All multiplicative bonuses apply only to proved samples, keeping the prove-rate floor intact.
Each RL condition uses seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ and identical training data.
An earlier convex formulation ($\alpha r_{\text{exec}} + \beta r_{\text{exec}}\text{ISR}$, $\alpha{+}\beta{=}1$) was discarded because $\text{ISR}{<}1$ always penalized relative to exec-only, collapsing PR (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).

Across conditions, seeds, and logic types we identify eight structural-degeneration modes via automated classifiers (full definitions in Appendix~\ref{app:hacking-modes}): \textbf{conclusion embedding} (CE), \textbf{tautological shortcut} (TS; subtypes TS-a standard and TS-b obfuscated), \textbf{premise-subset gaming} (PG), tautological collapse, repetition collapse, complexity-without-utility, contradiction explosion, and query-as-fact gaming (Prolog-specific). A ninth mode, \textbf{contradiction injection} (CI), is identified through manual audit at 1.7B only.
Modes are identified by strict text matching (CE/TS) plus functional $n_{\text{necessary}}$ analysis, with classification priority TS $>$ CE $>$ PG $>$ residual (non-hacking); the taxonomy is independently applicable to any solver-backed system with inspectable premise--conclusion structure.

We distinguish two failure semantics: exec-only \emph{low} ISR signals \emph{redundancy}, whereas ISR-rewarded \emph{high} ISR signals \emph{metric gaming}; the mode breakdown, not bare ISR, licenses reasoning-quality conclusions.

We define \emph{strict non-hacking} (S-NH) as the intersection of non-hacking (matching none of the eight automated taxonomy modes) and content-dependent (using predicates derived from the natural-language premises rather than abstract placeholders).
This filters content-independent proofs that may evade the taxonomy through structural novelty; S-NH rates are reported for cross-scale comparisons (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}) where content independence is prevalent.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Task and GRPO Training}
\label{sec:task}

Given premises $P_1,\ldots,P_k$ and conclusion $C$, the task is to produce a formal program $x=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}$ verified by an external solver $S\in\{\text{Prover9}$~\citep{mccune-prover9}$, \text{SWI-Prolog}$~\citep{wielemaker2012swi}$\}$ .
We train with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}4$), where each rollout receives binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}(x) = \mathbf{1}[S(x){=}\textit{proved}]$.
This optimizes prove rate but provides no signal about \emph{structural quality}: a formalization embedding the conclusion among its premises receives the same reward as a faithful derivation.
All experiments draw from FOLIO~\citep{folio}; the held-out evaluation file retains a legacy \texttt{proofwriter\_fol\_*.jsonl} filename (from ProofWriter~\citep{proofwriter}) but contains only FOLIO-derived examples.

\subsection{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{sec:sta}

STA tests whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary for proof success .
Given a proved $x$ with $n$ components, STA constructs $n$ ablated variants $x\setminus\{c_i\}$ and re-runs the solver (Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta}).
A component is \emph{necessary} if its removal causes proof failure.
What constitutes a component depends on the logic: premises and conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent) in FOL, clauses or ground facts in Prolog.
For example, given premise $\forall x(R(x){\to}P(x))$ and conclusion $\forall x(P(x){\to}Q(x))$, the decomposition yields components $\{$premise, $\forall x$, $P(x)$, $Q(x)\}$ with $n{=}4$.
LOO ablation itself is standard in mutation testing and sensitivity analysis~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Proved formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE $\text{ISR}(x) \in [0, 1]$
\STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ to $n$}
    \IF{$S(x \setminus \{c_i\}) = \textit{failed}$}
        \STATE $\textit{necessary} \gets \textit{necessary} + 1$
    \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $\textit{necessary} \,/\, n$
\end{algorithmic}
\smallskip
{\footnotesize For FOL, components include both premises and conclusion sub-expressions (quantifier, antecedent, consequent); each sub-expression is ablated by removing it from the solver input and testing whether the proof still succeeds.}
\end{algorithm}

ISR is the fraction of necessary components:
\begin{equation}
  \text{ISR}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\bigl[S(x\setminus\{c_i\})=\textit{failed}\bigr]
  \label{eq:isr}
\end{equation}
ISR is defined only for proved formalizations: ISR${=}1$ means every component is necessary; ISR${=}0$ means complete redundancy.
ISR is a component-necessity diagnostic, not a reasoning-quality metric; it measures whether each piece is needed for the proof, not whether the proof faithfully represents the original problem.
We report \emph{proved-only} ISR (denoted ISR$^*$) throughout to avoid conflating structural quality with prove rate.

ISR measures syntactic component necessity, not semantic faithfulness: a formalization can achieve $\text{ISR}{=}1$ while remaining semantically unrelated to the NL input.
ISR is sensitive to component count $n$: fewer components mechanically inflate ISR because each is more likely to be individually necessary.
This confound is central to ISR's Goodhart vulnerability (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): TS tautologies (single premise $=$ conclusion) achieve $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$ by construction; premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the apparent ISR advantage ($1.06\times$; Appendix~\ref{app:extended-discussion}).
ISR functions as a diagnostic but fails as a training signal because optimization exploits the metric's structural bias rather than improving reasoning quality.

Shapley values~\citep{shapley-1953} account for interaction effects but cost $O(2^n)$; we chose LOO because it directly answers ``is this component necessary?'' at $O(n)$ cost.
A cheaper $O(1)$ binary variant produces near-zero ISR ($\text{ISR}^*{=}0.007$), confirming that per-clause LOO is necessary for ISR to carry a structural signal (Appendix~\ref{app:o1-ablation}).

\subsection{Reward Conditions and Hacking Modes}
\label{sec:rewards}
\label{sec:taxonomy-method}

We study six primary conditions.
The exec-only baseline uses binary execution reward $r_{\text{exec}}$ alone.
ISR reward augments execution with a structural bonus, $r = r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1{+}\beta\,\text{ISR})$, at primary doses $\beta\in\{0.1,0.3\}$ and supplementary points $\beta\in\{0.05,0.2\}$; matched random controls replace ISR with uniform noise ($r = r_{\text{exec}}\cdot(1{+}\beta u)$, $u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)$) to isolate ISR-specific signal from generic reward-variance effects.
An SFT baseline trained with negative log-likelihood on gold formalizations tests whether structural degeneration arises from RL optimization or data exposure.
All multiplicative bonuses apply only to proved samples, keeping the prove-rate floor intact.
Each RL condition uses seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ and identical training data.
An earlier convex formulation ($\alpha r_{\text{exec}} + \beta r_{\text{exec}}\text{ISR}$, $\alpha{+}\beta{=}1$) was discarded because $\text{ISR}{<}1$ always penalized relative to exec-only, collapsing PR (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).

Across conditions, seeds, and logic types we identify eight structural-degeneration modes via automated classifiers (full definitions in Appendix~\ref{app:hacking-modes}): \textbf{conclusion embedding} (CE), \textbf{tautological shortcut} (TS; subtypes TS-a standard and TS-b obfuscated), \textbf{premise-subset gaming} (PG), tautological collapse, repetition collapse, complexity-without-utility, contradiction explosion, and query-as-fact gaming (Prolog-specific). A ninth mode, \textbf{contradiction injection} (CI), is identified through manual audit at 1.7B only.
Modes are identified by strict text matching (CE/TS) plus functional $n_{\text{necessary}}$ analysis, with classification priority TS $>$ CE $>$ PG $>$ residual (non-hacking); the taxonomy is independently applicable to any solver-backed system with inspectable premise--conclusion structure.
CE and TS are robust modes validated across ${\geq}3$ seeds and multiple conditions; PG is observed across multiple seeds but at low prevalence (${\leq}8\%$ of proved samples); CI (contradiction injection) is identified via manual audit at 1.7B only; remaining modes (tautological, repetition, complexity-without-utility, contradiction, query-as-fact) are isolated single-seed observations.
We distinguish two failure semantics: exec-only \emph{low} ISR signals \emph{redundancy}, whereas ISR-rewarded \emph{high} ISR signals \emph{metric gaming}; the mode breakdown, not bare ISR, licenses reasoning-quality conclusions.

We define \emph{strict non-hacking} (S-NH) as the intersection of non-hacking (matching none of the eight automated taxonomy modes) and content-dependent (using predicates derived from the natural-language premises rather than abstract placeholders).
This filters content-independent proofs that may evade the taxonomy through structural novelty; S-NH rates are reported for cross-scale comparisons (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}) where content independence is prevalent.
All non-hacking rates reported without the ``strict'' qualifier are upper bounds: undiscovered gaming modes would reduce the true rate.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for solver-backed formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
This gap is especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback, driving rapid prove-rate gains but providing no signal on the structural necessity of individual components.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not directly apply to arbitrary solver-backed settings; while LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}, RL training produces qualitatively different failures because the optimizer actively reshapes the output distribution toward degenerate attractors.
What is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in solver-backed formal outputs.

We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs to test whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary.
The fraction of necessary components yields the \emph{Irreducible Solver Rate} (ISR), where $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicates full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate: ISR$^*$ falls to $0.03{\pm}0.05$ across three seeds at 1000 steps while prove rate rises to ${\geq}96\%$ (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
An SFT baseline on identical data largely avoids hacking, consistent with hacking being associated with RL optimization rather than data exposure, though the large prove-rate gap prevents definitive causal attribution (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
The mechanism is structural: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive high ISR by construction, creating an attractor that eventually captures all seeds under extended training.
The effect transfers to Prolog with complete collapse through three distinct mechanisms (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

We present an empirical case study of Goodhart collapse in solver-backed RL, using FOLIO with Qwen3 (4B/1.7B) across six reward conditions, ten seeds (5+5 matched design), two logic types, and up to 1000 training steps. Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]

  \item \textbf{Empirical characterization of Goodhart dynamics} under LOO-based rewards, including seed-dependent divergence, dose-varying patterns, and a taxonomy of eight automatically detected hacking modes plus one identified by manual audit (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}--\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate STA along three axes: ISR as a diagnostic for reward hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); ISR as a training reward across four dose levels, where it exhibits Goodhart effects (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); and STA as a cross-logic protocol (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
5	Cross-scale evidence from Qwen3-1.7B reveals capacity-dependent Goodhart basins (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}).
6	A hacking taxonomy synthesizes the modes observed across conditions (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
7	
8	\subsection{Setup}\label{sec:setup}
9	
10	We train Qwen3-4B~\citep{qwen3} with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}4$, lr $10^{-6}$, 500 steps default, 1000 where noted) over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ on a fixed 500-example FOLIO~\citep{folio} subset held constant across all conditions; the SFT baseline is trained with negative log-likelihood (NLL) on gold formalizations.\footnote{All experiments use \texttt{data/train\_500\_seed42.jsonl}; seeds control initialization and rollout sampling only.}
11	Held-out evaluation uses 100 FOLIO examples (\texttt{proofwriter\_fol\_100.jsonl}) with greedy decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}); training uses sampling ($T{=}0.7$), so evaluation reflects the mode of the learned distribution rather than the stochastic rollout behavior that drives RL updates.
12	We report prove rate (PR), proved-only ISR ($\text{ISR}^*$), and hacking-mode rates from a two-stage classifier (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method}): strict text matching for CE/TS, followed by functional analysis of $n_{\text{necessary}}$.
13	The \emph{non-hacking} (N-H) rate is the residual of proved samples matching none of the eight automatically cataloged patterns; a ninth mode, CI, is identified by manual audit (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
14	\emph{Strict non-hacking} further requires content-dependent predicates derived from the natural-language premises, filtering content-independent proofs that evade the taxonomy through structural novelty (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}).
15	
16	\subsection{ISR as Diagnostic}
17	\label{sec:diagnostic}
18	
19	\begin{figure}[t]
20	\centering
21	\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_isr_collapse.pdf}
22	\caption{ISR collapse under exec-only GRPO (seed~42). (a) Both metrics on the same $[0,1]$ scale: PR rises 32\%$\to$93\%$\to$96\% while ISR$^*$ falls $0.642{\to}0.132{\to}0.003$ over 100$\to$500$\to$1000 steps; the shaded region shows the growing divergence. (b) Hacking modes progressively replace non-hacking output: by step 1000, CE dominates 100\% of proved samples.}
23	\label{fig:isr-collapse}
24	\end{figure}
25	
26	\textbf{Collapse trajectory.}
27	Figure~\ref{fig:isr-collapse} traces exec-only GRPO (seed~42) at 100, 500, 1000 steps.
28	PR rises $32\%\to93\%\to96\%$, a trajectory that execution-only evaluation would interpret as successful optimization; $\text{ISR}^*$ tells the opposite story, $0.642\to0.132\to0.003$ (214$\times$ collapse). %% registry: plan003-eval-exec-only-r5, plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan016-extended-1000-s42
29	By 500 steps, 87.1\% of proved samples embed the conclusion (CE); by 1000 steps, the embedding rate saturates at 100\% and mean component count more than doubles ($6.58\to18.55$) as the model emits contradictory or vacuous premises that trivially derive any conclusion.
30	Extended training, lacking a structural signal, \emph{worsens} formalization quality while improving the headline number.
31	
32	\textbf{Cross-seed instability.}
33	The three exec-only seeds diverge into qualitatively different failure modes despite shared data, hyperparameters, and reward (Appendix~\ref{app:detailed-results}).
34	Seed~42 reaches $\text{PR}{=}93\%$ via conclusion embedding ($\text{CE}{=}87\%$); s43 collapses to $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ via repetition (87\% of rollouts truncated)\footnote{Exec-only s43 was evaluated with sampling ($T{=}0.7$) rather than greedy decoding; its metrics are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).}; s44 reaches $\text{PR}{=}98\%$ via tautological collapse ($\text{TS}{=}100\%$, mean $n{=}2.04$). %% registry: plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan001-exec-only-s43-r4, plan001-exec-only-s44
35	Cross-seed PR variance ($\sigma{=}47$\,pp) shows that aggregate metrics obscure qualitatively different failure modes. All three seeds are flagged by $\text{ISR}^*$, whether they pass the PR check (s44) or fail it (s43).
36	By 1000 steps, all three converge to high PR ($0.97{\pm}0.02$) with near-zero non-hacking output via different dominant modes (Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:exec-only-1000},~\ref{tab:fol-detailed}). %% registry: plan016-extended-1000-s42, exec-only-s43-1000step-r7, plan001-exec-only-s44-1000-r2
37	S43 recovers from $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ to $96\%$ entirely through CE exploitation: PR recovery does not imply quality recovery.
38	
39	\textbf{SFT baseline.}
40	SFT on gold formalizations reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps) with $92.3\%$ non-hacking ($n{=}39$; per-seed range ${\sim}$91--93\%).
41	TS is entirely absent; CE occurs at $7.7\%$ ($\text{OR}{=}147$ vs.\ exec-only, $p{<}0.001$). %% registry: plan009-sft-baseline-s42-1000/s43-1000/s44-1000-r3
42	The near-absence of hacking under identical data exposure is consistent with hacking being RL-specific; a 100-step checkpoint ($\text{PR}{=}32\%$, hacking${\geq}31\%$) partially controls for the PR-level confound (Appendix~\ref{app:100step}).
43	Exploit discovery requires the trial-and-error sampling inherent to RL but absent from supervised training; whether SFT would hack at higher PR remains an open question.
44	
45	\subsection{ISR as Reward: Goodhart Effects}
46	\label{sec:goodhart}
47

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate STA along three axes: ISR as a diagnostic for reward hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}); ISR as a training reward across four dose levels, where it exhibits Goodhart effects (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); and STA as a cross-logic protocol (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Cross-scale evidence from Qwen3-1.7B reveals capacity-dependent Goodhart basins (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}).
A hacking taxonomy synthesizes the modes observed across conditions (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\subsection{Setup}\label{sec:setup}

We train Qwen3-4B~\citep{qwen3} with GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} ($K{=}4$, lr $10^{-6}$, 500 steps default, 1000 where noted) over seeds $\{42,43,44\}$ on a fixed 500-example FOLIO~\citep{folio} subset held constant across all conditions; the SFT baseline is trained with negative log-likelihood (NLL) on gold formalizations.\footnote{All experiments use \texttt{data/train\_500\_seed42.jsonl}; seeds control initialization and rollout sampling only.}
Held-out evaluation uses 100 FOLIO examples (\texttt{proofwriter\_fol\_100.jsonl}) with greedy decoding (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}); training uses sampling ($T{=}0.7$), so evaluation reflects the mode of the learned distribution rather than the stochastic rollout behavior that drives RL updates.
We report prove rate (PR), proved-only ISR ($\text{ISR}^*$), and hacking-mode rates from a two-stage classifier (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy-method}): strict text matching for CE/TS, followed by functional analysis of $n_{\text{necessary}}$.
The \emph{non-hacking} (N-H) rate is the residual of proved samples matching none of the eight automatically cataloged patterns; a ninth mode, CI, is identified by manual audit (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).
\emph{Strict non-hacking} further requires content-dependent predicates derived from the natural-language premises, filtering content-independent proofs that evade the taxonomy through structural novelty (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}).

\subsection{ISR as Diagnostic}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering

\caption{ISR collapse under exec-only GRPO (seed~42). (a) Both metrics on the same $[0,1]$ scale: PR rises 32\%$\to$93\%$\to$96\% while ISR$^*$ falls $0.642{\to}0.132{\to}0.003$ over 100$\to$500$\to$1000 steps; the shaded region shows the growing divergence. (b) Hacking modes progressively replace non-hacking output: by step 1000, CE dominates 100\% of proved samples.}
\label{fig:isr-collapse}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Collapse trajectory.}
Figure~\ref{fig:isr-collapse} traces exec-only GRPO (seed~42) at 100, 500, 1000 steps.
PR rises $32\%\to93\%\to96\%$, a trajectory that execution-only evaluation would interpret as successful optimization; $\text{ISR}^*$ tells the opposite story, $0.642\to0.132\to0.003$ (214$\times$ collapse). %% registry: plan003-eval-exec-only-r5, plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan016-extended-1000-s42
By 500 steps, 87.1\% of proved samples embed the conclusion (CE); by 1000 steps, the embedding rate saturates at 100\% and mean component count more than doubles ($6.58\to18.55$) as the model emits contradictory or vacuous premises that trivially derive any conclusion.
Extended training, lacking a structural signal, \emph{worsens} formalization quality while improving the headline number.

\textbf{Cross-seed instability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge into qualitatively different failure modes despite shared data, hyperparameters, and reward (Appendix~\ref{app:detailed-results}).
Seed~42 reaches $\text{PR}{=}93\%$ via conclusion embedding ($\text{CE}{=}87\%$); s43 collapses to $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ via repetition (87\% of rollouts truncated)\footnote{Exec-only s43 was evaluated with sampling ($T{=}0.7$) rather than greedy decoding; its metrics are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable (Appendix~\ref{app:setup}).}; s44 reaches $\text{PR}{=}98\%$ via tautological collapse ($\text{TS}{=}100\%$, mean $n{=}2.04$). %% registry: plan001-exec-only-s42-r2, plan001-exec-only-s43-r4, plan001-exec-only-s44
Cross-seed PR variance ($\sigma{=}47$\,pp) shows that aggregate metrics obscure qualitatively different failure modes. All three seeds are flagged by $\text{ISR}^*$, whether they pass the PR check (s44) or fail it (s43).
By 1000 steps, all three converge to high PR ($0.97{\pm}0.02$) with near-zero non-hacking output via different dominant modes (Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:exec-only-1000},~\ref{tab:fol-detailed}). %% registry: plan016-extended-1000-s42, exec-only-s43-1000step-r7, plan001-exec-only-s44-1000-r2
S43 recovers from $\text{PR}{=}13\%$ to $96\%$ entirely through CE exploitation: PR recovery does not imply quality recovery.

\textbf{SFT baseline.}
SFT on gold formalizations reaches $\text{PR}{=}13.0\%$ (3-seed pooled, 1000 steps) with $92.3\%$ non-hacking ($n{=}39$; per-seed range ${\sim}$91--93\%).
TS is entirely absent; CE occurs at $7.7\%$ ($\text{OR}{=}147$ vs.\ exec-only, $p{<}0.001$). %% registry: plan009-sft-baseline-s42-1000/s43-1000/s44-1000-r3

Exploit discovery requires the trial-and-error sampling inherent to RL but absent from supervised training; whether SFT would hack at higher PR remains an open question.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Prove rate, the dominant evaluation metric for solver-backed formalizers~\citep{logic-lm, linc, satlm}, conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts.
This gap is especially consequential under RL, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\citep{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\citep{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback, driving rapid prove-rate gains but providing no signal on the structural necessity of individual components.
Process reward models~\citep{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} require expensive annotations and do not directly apply to arbitrary solver-backed settings; while LLMs already game logical formalization at inference time~\citep{kim-game-formalization, bondarenko-spec-gaming}, RL training produces qualitatively different failures because the optimizer actively reshapes the output distribution toward degenerate attractors.
What is missing is an annotation-free \emph{diagnostic} for structural integrity in solver-backed formal outputs.

We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), which applies leave-one-out ablation on solver inputs to test whether each component of a proved formalization is individually necessary.
The fraction of necessary components yields the \emph{Irreducible Solver Rate} (ISR), where $\text{ISR}{=}1$ indicates full necessity and $\text{ISR}{=}0$ complete redundancy.
LOO ablation itself is standard~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in applying it as a GRPO-hacking diagnostic and in the empirical phenomena it surfaces.
As a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\citep{folio}, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory invisible to prove rate: ISR$^*$ falls to $0.03{\pm}0.05$ across three seeds at 1000 steps while prove rate rises to ${\geq}96\%$ (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
An SFT baseline on identical data largely avoids hacking, consistent with hacking being associated with RL optimization rather than data exposure, though the large prove-rate gap prevents definitive causal attribution (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

The mechanism is structural: tautological proofs (a single premise identical to the conclusion) receive high ISR by construction, creating an attractor that eventually captures all seeds under extended training.
The effect transfers to Prolog with complete collapse through three distinct mechanisms (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
ISR's asymmetry is the central finding: \emph{reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer at any dose.}

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation, and ISR exhibits Goodhart collapse at all four tested doses.
The core asymmetry is that the same LOO structure making ISR a useful diagnostic also makes it a vulnerable optimization target: tautological constructions satisfy component necessity by definition.
An SFT baseline largely avoids hacking under identical data, consistent with hacking being associated with RL optimization, though the prove-rate gap (13\% vs.\ 97\%) prevents definitive causal attribution.
Any transient non-hacking window ($p{=}0.92$, permutation test; matched 5+5 design) disappears under extended training; snapshot evaluation overestimates ISR's benefit.

All experiments use Qwen3 (4B/1.7B), FOLIO, and GRPO; the structural vulnerability follows from the LOO definition and should in principle transfer to settings where the optimizer can reduce component count.
Our results illustrate regressional Goodhart~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: structural diagnostics should remain decoupled from the training loop.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate Fig 5: Training ISR curves across reward conditions — meta-Goodhart gaming."""

import json
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

OI_BLUE = "#0072B2"
OI_RED  = "#D55E00"
OI_SKY  = "#56B4E9"
OI_GREY = "#999999"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "DejaVu Sans", "font.size": 8,
    "axes.titlesize": 9, "axes.labelsize": 8,
    "xtick.labelsize": 7.5, "ytick.labelsize": 7.5,
    "legend.fontsize": 7, "figure.dpi": 300,
    "savefig.dpi": 300, "savefig.bbox": "tight",
    "savefig.pad_inches": 0.03,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.4, "pdf.fonttype": 42, "ps.fonttype": 42,
})


def rolling_mean(arr, w=20):
    kernel = np.ones(w) / w
    padded = np.concatenate([np.full(w - 1, arr[0]), arr])
    return np.convolve(padded, kernel, mode="valid")


data_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "fig2_data.json")
with open(data_path) as f:
    data = json.load(f)

W = 20

exec_s44_steps = np.array(data["exec_s44"]["steps"])
exec_s44_smooth = rolling_mean(np.array(data["exec_s44"]["isr"]), W)

isr_s44_steps = np.array(data["isr_s44"]["steps"])
isr_s44_smooth = rolling_mean(np.array(data["isr_s44"]["isr"]), W)

isr_1k_steps = np.array(data["isr_s42_1000"]["steps"])
isr_1k_smooth = rolling_mean(np.array(data["isr_s42_1000"]["isr"]), W)

rand_s44_steps = np.array(data["random_s44"]["steps"])
rand_s44_smooth = rolling_mean(np.array(data["random_s44"]["isr"]), W)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.25, 2.4))

ax.plot(isr_s44_steps, isr_s44_smooth, color=OI_RED, linewidth=1.6,
        label=r"ISR $\beta\!=\!0.1$ (s44)", zorder=5)
ax.plot(isr_1k_steps, isr_1k_smooth, color=OI_RED, linewidth=1.0,
        alpha=0.5, linestyle="--",
        label=r"ISR $\beta\!=\!0.1$ (s42, 1k)", zorder=4)

ax.plot(exec_s44_steps, exec_s44_smooth, color=OI_BLUE, linewidth=1.6,
        label="Exec-only (s44)", zorder=5)

ax.plot(rand_s44_steps, rand_s44_smooth, color=OI_SKY, linewidth=1.6,
        label=r"Random $\beta\!=\!0.1$ (s44)", zorder=5)

collapse_step = 280
collapse_isr = isr_s44_smooth[collapse_step - 1]
ax.annotate("Goodhart\ncollapse",
            xy=(collapse_step, collapse_isr),
            xytext=(80, 0.92),
            fontsize=6.5, color=OI_RED, fontweight="bold",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=OI_RED, lw=0.8,
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.2"),
            ha="center", va="center")

ax.annotate("TS artifact",
            xy=(350, exec_s44_smooth[349]),
            xytext=(430, 0.65),
            fontsize=7.5, color=OI_BLUE, fontstyle="italic",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=OI_BLUE, lw=0.7,
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.2"),
            ha="center", va="center")

ax.set_xlabel("Training Step")
ax.set_ylabel("Training ISR (rolling mean, $w$=20)")
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1050)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.0), framealpha=1.0,
          edgecolor="#CCCCCC", fontsize=8, handlelength=1.5, borderpad=0.5)
ax.yaxis.grid(True, alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)

out_dir = os.path.dirname(__file__)
for ext in ("pdf", "png"):
    out = os.path.join(out_dir, f"fig5_training_isr_curves.{ext}")
    fig.savefig(out, format=ext)
    print(f"Saved: {out}")
plt.close()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate Fig 2: Exec-only ISR collapse — PR rises while ISR* collapses.

Redesign: single Y-axis (both metrics on [0,1]), fill_between divergence,
collapse zone shading. Removes L1-violating dual Y-axis.
"""

import os
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patheffects as pe
import numpy as np

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "DejaVu Sans", "font.size": 11,
    "axes.titlesize": 13, "axes.labelsize": 12,
    "xtick.labelsize": 10, "ytick.labelsize": 10,
    "legend.fontsize": 10, "figure.dpi": 300,
    "savefig.dpi": 300, "savefig.bbox": "tight",
    "savefig.pad_inches": 0.05,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.8, "pdf.fonttype": 42, "ps.fonttype": 42,
})

C_PR   = "#0072B2"
C_ISR  = "#D55E00"
C_TS   = "#D55E00"
C_CE   = "#E69F00"
C_PG   = "#56B4E9"
C_GEN  = "#009E73"

# ── Data (exec-only seed 42) ──
steps    = [0, 100, 500, 1000]
pr_vals  = [0.12, 0.32, 0.93, 0.96]
isr_vals = [0.064, 0.642, 0.132, 0.003]

# Taxonomy (steps 100, 500, 1000)
tax_steps = [100, 500, 1000]
tax_n     = [32, 93, 96]
tax_h7a   = [28.1, 0.0, 0.0]
tax_h1    = [3.1, 87.1, 100.0]
tax_h8    = [0.0, 5.4, 0.0]
tax_gen   = [68.8, 7.5, 0.0]

fig, (ax_top, ax_bot) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(7, 6.8),
    gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.2, 1]},
)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.35, bottom=0.1)

# ════════════════════════════════════════════
# (a) Top panel: single Y-axis, both on [0,1]
# ════════════════════════════════════════════

# Collapse zone (Pattern A)
ax_top.axhspan(0, 0.10, color="#FDEDEC", alpha=0.5, zorder=0)
t = ax_top.text(950, 0.05, "collapse zone", fontsize=8,
                color="#ccaaaa", fontstyle="italic", ha="right", va="center")
t.set_path_effects([pe.withStroke(linewidth=2.5, foreground="white")])

# Divergence fill (Pattern B)
steps_arr = np.array(steps)
pr_arr = np.array(pr_vals)
isr_arr = np.array(isr_vals)
from scipy.interpolate import make_interp_spline

    x_smooth = np.linspace(0, 1000, 200)
    spl_pr = make_interp_spline(steps_arr, pr_arr, k=2)
    spl_isr = make_interp_spline(steps_arr, isr_arr, k=2)
    pr_smooth = np.clip(spl_pr(x_smooth), 0, 1)
    isr_smooth = np.clip(spl_isr(x_smooth), 0, 1)
    ax_top.fill_between(x_smooth, pr_smooth, isr_smooth,
                        alpha=0.06, color="#555555", zorder=1)
except ImportError:
    ax_top.fill_between(steps, pr_vals, isr_vals,
                        alpha=0.06, color="#555555", zorder=1, step="mid")

ax_top.plot(steps, pr_vals, color=C_PR, marker="o", markersize=7,
            linewidth=2.2, label="Prove Rate", zorder=5,
            markeredgecolor="white", markeredgewidth=1.0)
ax_top.plot(steps, isr_vals, color=C_ISR, marker="s", markersize=7,
            linewidth=2.2, linestyle="--", label="ISR*", zorder=5,
            markeredgecolor="white", markeredgewidth=1.0)

# Direct labels (L1: direct annotation > legend when possible)
ax_top.annotate("96%", xy=(1000, 0.96), xytext=(920, 0.88),
                fontsize=9, color=C_PR, fontweight="bold",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=C_PR, lw=0.6))
ax_top.annotate("0.003", xy=(1000, 0.003), xytext=(880, 0.14),
                fontsize=9, color=C_ISR, fontweight="bold",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=C_ISR, lw=0.6))

ax_top.set_xlabel("Training Step")
ax_top.set_ylabel("Metric Value")
ax_top.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.05)
ax_top.set_xlim(-50, 1080)
ax_top.set_xticks(steps)
ax_top.legend(loc="center right", framealpha=0.9, edgecolor="none")
ax_top.yaxis.grid(True, alpha=0.2, linewidth=0.5)
ax_top.set_title("(a) PR rises while ISR* collapses to zero", fontsize=13)

# ════════════════════════════════════════════
# (b) Bottom panel: stacked bar taxonomy
# ════════════════════════════════════════════
x = np.arange(len(tax_steps))
bar_w = 0.5

bottom = np.zeros(len(tax_steps))
kw = dict(width=bar_w, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5, zorder=3)

ax_bot.bar(x, tax_h7a, bottom=bottom, color=C_TS, label="TS tautological", **kw)
bottom = np.array(tax_h7a)
ax_bot.bar(x, tax_h1, bottom=bottom, color=C_CE, label="CE shortcut", **kw)
bottom += np.array(tax_h1)
ax_bot.bar(x, tax_h8, bottom=bottom, color=C_PG, label="PG conjunction", **kw)
bottom += np.array(tax_h8)
ax_bot.bar(x, tax_gen, bottom=bottom, color=C_GEN, label="Non-hacking", **kw)

for i in range(len(tax_steps)):
    ax_bot.text(x[i], 102, f"n={tax_n[i]}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=9, color="#444444")

ax_bot.set_xticks(x)
ax_bot.set_xticklabels([f"Step {s}" for s in tax_steps])
ax_bot.set_ylabel("Percentage (%)")
ax_bot.set_ylim(0, 112)
ax_bot.set_yticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
ax_bot.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower center", frameon=False, ncol=4,
              bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22))
ax_bot.set_title("(b) Non-hacking output vanishes as hacking modes dominate", fontsize=13)

# ── Save ──
out_dir = os.path.dirname(__file__)
for ext in ("pdf", "png"):
    out = os.path.join(out_dir, f"fig2_isr_collapse.{ext}")
    fig.savefig(out, format=ext)
    print(f"Saved: {out}")
plt.close()

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Formal reasoning with LLMs.}
LLM-solver pipelines~\citep{satlm, logic-lm, linc, fover-pei2025, lorp} and RL methods on solver feedback~\citep{polu2020generative, zelikman2022star, mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, deepseek-prover-v15, deepseek-prover-v2, deepseek-r1-2025} evaluate execution accuracy alone; math-specialized models such as Llemma~\citep{azerbayev2024llemma} similarly rely on downstream task accuracy without structural diagnostics.
We use FOLIO~\citep{folio}, the only public NLI benchmark with both FOL and Prolog annotations.

\paragraph{Faithfulness in formalization.}
\citet{kim-game-formalization} study whether GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 game Lean~4 formalization at \emph{inference} time. Using axiom diffing and LLM-judge classification on 303 FOL problems, they find no systematic gaming in unified generation but identify two unfaithfulness modes: axiom fabrication during proof (56\% are conclusion-as-axiom) and premise mistranslation during formalization.
Our work differs in three respects.
First, we study \emph{training-time} gaming under GRPO, where the optimizer actively reshapes the output distribution, producing qualitatively different failures from one-shot inference.
Second, our detection method (STA/ISR) is deterministic and solver-derived, requiring no LLM judge.
Third, we observe universal gaming under RL (all GRPO conditions show ${\geq}80\%$ hacking), whereas Kim et al.\ report that models prefer failure over forcing proofs at inference time.
The complementarity is direct: their axiom-fabrication mode is functionally equivalent to our CE (conclusion embedding), confirming that the same exploit class arises independently under both inference and training regimes.

\paragraph{Process rewards and reward shaping.}
PRMs~\citep{cobbe2021training, lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback but suffer from noise and distribution shift~\citep{processbench, zeng2025versaprm, khalifa2025thinkprm}. \citet{uesato2022solving} and \citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} show auxiliary rewards can \emph{hurt} RL training, a finding our ISR results corroborate.
Unlike potential-based shaping~\citep{ng1999policy}, ISR rewards output properties rather than state transitions, explaining its Goodhart vulnerability.
Symbolic feedback~\citep{rlsf} and interleaved verification bonuses~\citep{cao2026pushing} operate at token or step level; ISR operates at the component level (LOO ablation), and our results show this signal is gamed when optimized.
Rubric-grounded GRPO~\citep{rubric-grpo} uses structured LLM-judge rewards; ISR is solver-derived and deterministic but shares the proxy risk of reward augmentation.

\paragraph{Reward hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Goodhart's Law~\citep{goodhart-1975} is established theoretically~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl, everitt2021reward} and empirically in RLHF~\citep{amodei2016concrete, gao-reward-overoptimization, bondarenko-spec-gaming, kim-game-formalization, metr-reward-hacking, spurious-rewards}, text generation~\citep{paulus2018deep}, and deep RL~\citep{langosco2022goal, krakovna2020specification}.
\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} show heavy-tailed misspecification causes catastrophic Goodhart where KL regularization fails, consistent with ISR collapse under GRPO.
TRACE~\citep{wang2025trace} detects hacking via reasoning effort; STA measures structural necessity, a complementary axis.
Our setting differs from prior work in that ISR is deterministic and solver-derived, gaming emerges during training rather than at inference~\citep{geirhos2020shortcut, kim-game-formalization}, and the diagnostic itself becomes the optimization target.
\citet{pan-reward-misspecification} show more capable agents exploit misspecifications more severely; our cross-scale comparison complements this with qualitatively different exploits at 4B vs.\ 1.7B.
We frame our results as primarily regressional Goodhart~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: ISR's LOO definition creates structural bias toward tautology, with collapse at all four tested doses.
GRPO~\citep{deepseekmath} was introduced for mathematical reasoning, where binary correctness signals suffice because solution equivalence is well-defined; in formal logic, however, execution correctness does not imply structural faithfulness, creating the proxy gap that STA exposes.
STA adapts the LOO mutation paradigm~\citep{demillo1978, jia-harman-survey}; our contribution lies in the application and empirical findings.

4	Experiments use a single model family (Qwen3-4B/1.7B), one dataset (FOLIO, 500 train / 100 eval examples), and one RL algorithm (GRPO); generalization of specific hacking modes to other architectures or benchmarks remains open.
